links.outcome: Rate of LLMs giving inappropriate antibiotic advice, including after misinformation prompts
links.effect: 76.2% of responses were guideline-concordant; 6.6% unprompted overprescribing; 17.3% influenced by misinformation; some models were more vulnerable than others.
links.quote: Overall, 76.2% of responses were guideline-concordant, while 6.6% showed unprompted overprescribing and 17.3% were influenced by misinformation.

links.outcome: Frequency of AI antibiotic advice that is incorrect and would need clinician verification
links.effect: 6.6% unprompted overprescribing and 17.3% misinformation-influenced overprescribing, many involving broad-spectrum antibiotics.
links.quote: Many inappropriate prescriptions involved broad-spectrum antibiotics.

links.outcome: Inclusion of safety behaviors (advise consulting a doctor, warn against self-medication) in responses
links.effect: Fewer responses advised consulting a doctor, and warnings against self-medication were rare.
links.quote: Although most responses correctly noted that antibiotics do not treat viral infections, fewer advised consulting a doctor, and warnings against self-medication were rare.

screen.reason: Empirical evaluation of 5 commercial LLMs on 1,000 simulated clinical vignettes testing vulnerability to patient misinformation and adherence to antibiotic guidelines, but without testing a specific organizational safeguard or deployment intervention.
